title: You Can't Pour From an Empty Cup
hook: Looking after yourself isn't a luxury — it's part of caring for your baby. A rested, supported parent has more patience and presence to give.
key_points: A depleted parent runs on empty; taking care of yourself helps you take care of your baby.
Cover the basics — sleep when you can, eat, hydrate — and grab small breaks, even brief ones, early on.
Accept help, and automate or delegate what you can; you don't have to do everything perfectly.
Watch for burnout — resentment, exhaustion, feeling trapped — and reach out for support if it builds.
content_html: When you're caring for a baby around the clock, your own needs can feel like the first thing to drop — but a depleted parent runs on empty. The AAP puts it plainly: the best way to take care of your family is to make sure you're taking care of yourself, too. Your wellbeing is part of your baby's care.
extra_html: HealthyChildren.org suggests covering the basics — sleep when you can, eat, and stay hydrated — and carving out small breaks early on so you don't end up feeling trapped or resentful. You don't have to do everything perfectly; pick your real priorities, and automate or delegate the rest. Accept help when it's offered, and ask for it when it isn't. Watch for signs of burnout like building resentment and deep exhaustion. This is general guidance — if low mood, anxiety, or burnout linger or interfere with daily life, reach out to your doctor; if you have thoughts of harming yourself or the baby, seek help immediately.

related.title: Baby Blues or Something More?
related.hook: Weepy and overwhelmed in the first days is common and usually passes within two weeks. When low mood lingers and disrupts daily life, it may be postpartum depression — common and treatable.

related.title: Your Relationship After Baby
related.hook: A new baby tests even strong relationships. Sharing the load, talking honestly, and working as a team — while expecting routines and intimacy to shift for a while — helps you weather it together.

flashcards.prompt: Why does parental self-care matter for the baby?

choices.text: A rested, supported parent has more patience and presence to give
It doesn't — the baby's needs always come first, full stop
Only the baby's routine affects the baby

flashcards.explanation_html: The AAP frames self-care as part of caring for your child: you can't pour from an empty cup, and looking after yourself helps you parent well.

flashcards.prompt: What are some practical ways to care for yourself as a new parent?
flashcards.back_html: Cover the basics (sleep when you can, eat, hydrate), take small breaks early on, accept help, and automate or delegate tasks instead of chasing perfection.

choices.text: Feeling rested and patient most days
Enjoying short breaks away from the baby

flashcards.explanation_html: Neglecting your own needs can build into resentment and exhaustion. Noticing it early and reaching out for support helps.
